Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 95, verse 1:

Tafsir of Surat "Al-Tin" (The Fig). It is Meccan according to the majority. Ibn 'Abbas and Qatadah said: it is Madani, and it has eight verses.

In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate.

In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate.

By the fig and the olive. (1)

On this there are three issues.

The first: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿By the fig and the olive﴾. Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan, Mujahid, 'Ikrimah, Ibrahim al-Nakha'i, 'Ata' ibn Abi Rabah, Jabir ibn Zayd, Muqatil and al-Kalbi said: it is your fig which you eat, and your olive from which you press oil. Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿And a tree that grows out of Mount Sinai, which produces oil and a condiment for those who eat﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 20]. Abu Dharr said: A basket of figs was presented to the Prophet ﷺ, and he said: "Eat." And he ate from it. Then he said: "If I were to say that a fruit had come down from Paradise, I would say it is this, for the fruit of Paradise has no pits (ajam), so eat it, for it cuts off hemorrhoids and benefits gout." [The ajam (with a vowel on the first letter): the pits.] And it is narrated from Mu'adh that he used the siwak of an olive stick, and said: I heard the Prophet ﷺ say: "The siwak is the olive, from the blessed tree; it sweetens the mouth and removes phlegm, and it is my siwak and the siwak of the prophets before me."

It is also narrated from Ibn 'Abbas: the fig is the Mosque of Nuh (peace be upon him) which was built on al-Judi, and the olive is the Mosque of Bayt al-Maqdis. Al-Dahhak said: the fig is the Sacred Mosque, and the olive is the Farthest Mosque. Ibn Zayd: the fig is the Mosque of Damascus, and the olive is the Mosque of Bayt al-Maqdis. Qatadah: the fig is the mountain on which Damascus lies, and the olive is the mountain on which Bayt al-Maqdis lies. Muhammad ibn Ka'b said: the fig is the mosque of the People of the Cave, and the olive is the mosque of Iliya'. Ka'b al-Ahbar, Qatadah also, 'Ikrimah and Ibn Zayd said: the fig is Damascus, and the olive is Bayt al-Maqdis. This is the choice of al-Tabari. Al-Farra' said: I heard a man from the people of al-Sham say: the fig is the mountains between Hulwan and Hamadhan, and the olive is the mountains of al-Sham. It was also said: they are two mountains in al-Sham, called Tur Zayta and Tur Tina (in Syriac), named so because they produce them. Abu Makin narrated likewise from 'Ikrimah, who said: the fig and the olive are two mountains in al-Sham.

And al-Nabigha said:

... "They came to the fig from one side" [The line in full, as in the Kitab al-Malahin of Ibn Duraid and Shu'ara' al-Nasraniyya:

Sahb al-zilal atayna al-tin 'an 'urad... yuzjina ghaiman qalilan ma'uhu shabiman

Al-sahb and al-sahba: redness. Al-'arad: the crossing or the side. Yuzjina: they drive. Al-shabam: cold. The line describes clouds with no water in them. The author attributed it to Zuhayr.]

This is the name of a place. It is possible that this is by omission of a noun, meaning "and the places where the fig and the olive grow." But there is no evidence for that from the apparent text of the revelation, nor from the words of one who does not permit otherwise, said al-Nahhas.

The second: The soundest of these views is the first, because it is the literal meaning, and one does not turn from the literal to the figurative except with evidence. Allah swore by the fig because it was the covering of Adam in the Garden, based on His saying, exalted is He: ﴿They began to stick leaves of the Garden over themselves﴾ [al-A'raf: 22], and it was fig leaves. It was also said: He swore by it to show the great blessing in it, for it is beautiful in appearance, pleasant in taste, fragrant in smell, easy to pick, and of the size of a morsel. The poet has said well about it:

Look at the fig on the branches in the morning, its skin torn, its neck bent,
As if it were a lord of blessing that was stripped, then returned after being new in creation.
The smallest of its breasts is its largest, but it is called out in the streets.

And another said:

The fig, to me, equals every fruit when it bends, leaning on its bright branch,
Its face scratched, its sweetness flowing, as if it were bowing from fear of Allah.

And He swore by the olive because Ibrahim gave it as a parable in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿It is lit from a blessed tree, an olive﴾ [al-Nur: 35]. See vol. 12, p. 263. It is the most common condiment of the people of al-Sham and the Maghrib, who dip in it (yastabighuna, i.e., use it as relish), use it in their cooking, burn it for light, and it is used to treat ailments of the belly, sores and wounds, and it has many benefits. The Prophet ﷺ said: "Eat the oil and anoint yourselves with it, for it is from a blessed tree." The discussion of it has passed in Surat al-Mu'minun. See vol. 12, p. 116.

The third: Ibn al-'Arabi said: For the sake of the Creator, glory be to Him, the favour of the fig is magnified, and that it is a staple food that can be stored, therefore we say that zakat is obligatory on it. Many scholars have only refrained from explicitly stating the obligation of zakat on it out of fear of the oppression of the rulers, for they exceed their bounds regarding zakat wealth, taking it as a fine, just as the Truthful one ﷺ warned. So the scholars disliked giving them a way to another kind of wealth in which they might overstep. Yet a person should give thanks for his Lord's blessing by paying its due. Al-Shafi'i said, for this reason and others: there is no zakat on olives. But the sound view is that zakat is obligatory on both.

Ibn Abi Najih narrated from Mujahid that he said of "Tur" that it is a mountain, and of "Sinin" that it means "blessed" in Syriac. From Ikrimah, from Ibn Abbas, he said: "Tur" is a mountain, and "Sinin" means "good." Qatadah said: "Sinin" is "the blessed, the good." From Ikrimah, he said: it is the mountain from which Allah, exalted is His praise, called out to Musa, peace be upon him. Muqatil and al-Kalbi said: "Sinin" is every mountain on which there are fruit-bearing trees, so it is "Sinin" and "Sina'," in the language of the Nabataeans.

From Amr ibn Maymun, he said: I prayed the night prayer (al-'Isha') with Umar ibn al-Khattab in Makkah, and he recited ﴿By the fig and the olive﴾ ﴿and Mount Sinai﴾ ﴿and this secure city﴾. He said: Thus it is in the recitation of Abd Allah (Ibn Mas'ud), and he raised his voice in glorifying the House. In the second rak'ah he recited ﴿Have you not considered how your Lord dealt﴾ and ﴿for the security of the Quraysh﴾, combining the two. Ibn al-Anbari mentioned this.

Al-Nahhas said: In the recitation (qira'a, a variant mode of reciting the Qur'an) of Abd Allah it is "Sina'" with a kasra on the sin, while in the hadith of Amr ibn Maymun from Umar it is with a fatha on the sin.

Al-Akhfash said: "Tur" is a mountain, and "Sinin" is a tree whose singular is "Sinīniyya."

Abu Ali said: "Sinin" is of the pattern فِعْلِيل (fi'lil), so the lam, which is a nun, was repeated within it, just as it was repeated in "zihlil" (for a slippery place), "kirdida" (for a piece of dates), and "khindid" (for a tall person). "Sinin" is not declined with tanwin (ghayr munsarif, diptote), just as "Sina'" is not, because it was made the name of a plot or land. Had it been made the name of a place or a dwelling, or a masculine proper name, it would have been declined, because you would have named a masculine thing with a masculine thing.

Allah swore by this mountain only because it is in al-Sham and in the Holy Land, and Allah has blessed both, as He said: ﴿to the farthest mosque, whose surroundings We have blessed﴾.

It means Makkah. He called it "secure" (amin) because it is safe (aman), as He said: ﴿Have We not made a sanctuary secure?﴾ [Al-Ankabut: 67]. So "al-amin" carries the meaning of "al-aamin" (the safe one). This was said by al-Farra' and others. The poet said:

Do you not know, O Asma', woe be to you, that I have sworn an oath that I will not betray my trust (amini)?

That is, "my safety" (amini). On this basis, those who said that by "the fig" He meant Damascus, and by "the olive" Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem), argued as follows: God swore by the mountain of Damascus, because it is the abode of Jesus, peace be upon him, and by the mountain of Bayt al-Maqdis, because it is the station of the prophets, peace be upon them, and by Makkah, because it is the trace of Ibrahim and the home of Muhammad (ﷺ).

**Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on Surah 95, verses 4–5:**

There are two issues here.

**The first issue** concerns the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, We created man in the best of stature﴾. This is the answer to the oath. By "man" (al-insan) is meant the disbeliever. It is said that he is al-Walid ibn al-Mughira, and it is said that he is Kaldah ibn Usayd. On this view, the verse was revealed concerning those who denied the Resurrection (al-ba'th). It is also said that by "man" is meant Adam and his descendants. "In the best of stature" means in balance and the soundness of his form, as the majority of the exegetes (mufassirun) said. He is in the best state, because He created every other creature bent over with its face downward, while He created man upright, with an eloquent tongue and fingers with which he grasps. Abu Bakr ibn Tahir said: adorned with reason, able to carry out commands, guided by discernment, tall of stature, taking his food with his hand. Ibn al-'Arabi said: "There is no creation of Allah the Exalted more beautiful than man, for Allah created him living, knowing, capable, willing, speaking, hearing, seeing, and wise in management. These are the attributes of the Lord, glory be to Him, and some scholars alluded to this, and the explanation came in the saying [of the Prophet (ﷺ)]: [Allah created Adam in His image, meaning in His attributes which we have mentioned. And in another narration:] in the image of the Most Merciful. [And how can the Most Merciful have a distinct form? Nothing remains but that these are meanings]."

Al-Mubarak ibn 'Abd al-Jabbar al-Azdi informed us, saying: al-Qadi Abu al-Qasim 'Ali ibn Abi 'Ali al-Qadi al-Muhsin informed us, from his father, who said: 'Isa ibn Musa al-Hashimi loved his wife with an intense love. One day he said to her, "You are divorced three times if you are not more beautiful than the moon." She rose and veiled herself from him, and said, "You have divorced me!" He spent a great night of anguish. When morning came, he went to the house of al-Mansur and informed him of the matter, and he showed al-Mansur great distress. So al-Mansur summoned the jurists and asked them for a legal opinion. All who were present said, "She has been divorced," except one man from the companions of Abu Hanifa, who remained silent. Al-Mansur said to him, "Why do you not speak?" The man said to him: "In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Especially Merciful: ﴿By the fig and the olive, and Mount Sinai, and this secure city. Indeed, We created man in the best of stature﴾. O Commander of the Faithful, man is the best of things, and there is nothing better than him." Al-Mansur said to 'Isa ibn Musa, "The matter is as the man said, so turn to your wife." Abu Ja'far al-Mansur sent to the man's wife: "Obey your husband and do not disobey him, for he has not divorced you." This shows you that man is the best of Allah's creation, inwardly and outwardly, in beauty of form and wondrous composition: the head with what it contains, the chest with what it gathers, the belly with what it holds, the private parts with what they conceal, the two hands with what they seize, and the two feet with what they bear. For this reason the philosophers said that man is "the lesser world" (al-'alam al-asghar), since everything in the created beings is gathered in him. [[In some copies of the original and in Ibn al-'Arabi: (gathered in him).]]

**The second issue** concerns the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿Then We returned him to the lowest of the low﴾. That is, to the most abject age, which is senility after youth and weakness after strength, until he becomes like a child in his first state. This was said by al-Dahhak, al-Kalbi, and others. Ibn Abi Najih narrated from Mujahid: ﴿Then We returned him to the lowest of the low﴾ means to the Fire, meaning the disbeliever. Abu al-'Aliyah also said this. It is also said: when Allah described him with those sublime attributes with which man was constituted, he became arrogant and exalted himself, until he said, ﴿I am your Lord, the Most High﴾ [[Verse 24, Surah al-Nazi'at.]] [al-Nazi'at: 24]. When Allah knew this from His servant, and His decree proceeds from Him, He returned him to the lowest of the low, by making him filled with filth and laden with impurity, and by expelling it from his outer body in a disagreeable manner, sometimes by choice and sometimes by compulsion, until, when he witnesses that from his own condition, he returns to his proper measure. Abdullah read it as ﴿asfal as-safilin﴾ (with the definite article). He said "asfala safilin" in the plural, because "al-insan" carries the meaning of a plural. If he had said "asfala safil" (singular), it would have been permissible, because the word "al-insan" is singular. You say, "This is the best standing one" (hadha afdalu qa'im), and you do not say "afdalu qa'imin" (plural), because you are referring to one person. If the one being referred to is not a pronoun, its reference may be singular or plural, as in His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And he who brought the truth and confirmed it, those are the God-fearing﴾ [[Verse 33, Surah al-Zumar.]] [al-Zumar: 33]. And His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And when We let man taste mercy from Us, he rejoices in it; but if an evil befalls them﴾ [[Verse 48, Surah al-Shura.]] [al-Shura: 48]. It has also been said that the meaning of ﴿We returned him to the lowest of the low﴾ is that We returned him to misguidance, as He, the Exalted, said: ﴿Indeed, man is in loss, except those who have believed and done righteous deeds﴾. That is, except these, who are not returned to that. The exception (al-istithna') is connected (muttasil) according to the view of the one who said that "the lowest of the low" is the Fire. And according to the one who said it is senility, it is disconnected (munqati').

The Almighty's saying: ﴿Except those who believe and do righteous deeds﴾. Their good deeds are recorded for them and their evil deeds are erased from them. This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas. He said: they are those who reach old age; they are not held accountable for what they did in their old age.

Al-Dahhak narrated from him, saying: If a servant in his youth was abundant in prayer, abundant in fasting and charity, and then grew too weak for what he used to do in his youth, Allah, Mighty and Majestic, will continue to reward him for what he used to do in his youth. And in a hadith, the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "When a servant travels or falls ill, Allah records for him the same as what he used to do while resident and healthy." It was also said: ﴿Except those who believe and do righteous deeds﴾ means that they do not become senile and do not become decrepit, and the intellect of one who was knowledgeable and acted upon his knowledge does not depart. From Asim al-Ahwal, from Ikrimah, who said: Whoever recites the Qur'an will not be returned to the lowest age. It is related from Ibn 'Umar, from the Prophet (ﷺ), that he said: "Blessed is the one whose life is long and whose deeds are good." It is also related that when a believing servant dies, Allah commands his two angels [in some copies of the original: "angels"; in others: "two angels"] to worship at his grave until the Day of Resurrection, and that is recorded for him.

The Almighty's saying: ﴿So for them is a reward that will never be cut off﴾. Al-Dahhak said: a reward without deeds. And it was said: it is uninterrupted.

It was said: the address is to the disbeliever, as a rebuke and a confirmation of the proof, meaning: if you know, O man, that God created you in the best of forms, and that He will return you to the most abject age, and move you from one state to another, then what drives you to deny the resurrection and the recompense, when Muhammad (ﷺ) has told you of it?

And it was said: the address is to the Prophet (ﷺ), meaning: be certain, along with what has come to you from God, the Mighty and Majestic, that He is the most just of judges. This meaning is narrated from Qatada.

Qatada and al-Farra' also said: the meaning is, "Then who will deny you, O Messenger, after this clarification of the religion?" This is what al-Tabari chose. It is as if He said: "Who is able to do that, that is, to deny you of reward and punishment, after what has become evident of Our power to create man, and of the religion and the recompense?" The poet said:

*We subdued Tamim just as our forefathers did,*
*and their forefathers were subdued in the bygone age.*

(In the commentary of al-Shawkani, edition of Mustafa al-Babi al-Halabi (453: 5): "min salif al-zaman" ["in the bygone age"].)

Is not Allah the most just of judges? (Q. 95:8)

That is, the most perfect of judges in His making of all that He created. It was also said: "the most just of judges" in judgment with truth, and in justice among creation. In this there is an implication for those of the disbelievers who acknowledged an eternal Maker. When the interrogative alif enters a negation, and the sentence carries the sense of confirmation, it becomes an affirmation, as the poet said:

ألستم خير من ركب المطايا
Are you not the best of those who have ridden the mounts?

[From a qasidah of Jarir praising 'Abd al-Malik ibn Marwan. Its completion is:

وأندى العالمين بطون راح
"and the most generous of the worlds in bellies of wine."

[ ..... ]]

It was also said: "What then makes you deny the Judgement after this?" (Q. 95:7). "Is not Allah the most just of judges?" is abrogated by the verse of the sword (ayat al-sayf). It was also said: it is established, because there is no contradiction between them.

Ibn 'Abbas and 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with them both, when they recited "Is not Allah the most just of judges?", would say: "Yes indeed, and I am among the witnesses to that." And that is preferred. And Allah knows best.

Al-Tirmidhi narrated from Abu Hurayrah, who said: "Whoever recites Surat al-Tin wa al-Zaytun and comes to 'Is not Allah the most just of judges?' should say: 'Yes indeed, and I am among the witnesses to that.'" And Allah knows best.
